Rooftop hives: the quiet boom in urban beekeeping

From a distance, the glass towers of the City of London look like the last place a honeybee
would visit. Look closer, and more and more of them carry small wooden boxes on their roofs.
Amateur beekeepers have been moving their colonies upward since the start of the decade, and
several beekeeping societies report that membership has more than doubled since the middle of
the last decade.

The change began when a city corporation finally lifted a long-standing restriction on what
its buildings could host. Before rooftop hives were legalised in the capital in 2010,
would-be beekeepers had to drive their hives out beyond the ring road. After that, hives
appeared on office roofs, hotel terraces and even the occasional church spire. Many of the new
beekeepers say the rule change, not a surge of enthusiasm for honey, is what let the boom
happen.

By the numbers, the city suits the bee well. A city hive yields around 30 kg of honey a year,
against 20 kg for rural ones, according to figures collected by several beekeeping groups.
Urban plots draw on a wider variety of flowering plants — parks, balconies, railway
embankments — and there is no tractor spraying. The bees' foraging season stretches later into
the autumn, when town street planters are still in bloom.

City colonies appear to cope better with varroa, the parasitic mite blamed for much of the
decline in wild bees everywhere. Rural colonies do not escape the mite, but their cousins on
town roofs suffer less still; shorter winters and longer foraging seasons give the mites fewer
chances to get established.

Not everyone is cheering. Ecologist Dr Maya Renn has warned that the boom may be crowding out
wild pollinators, the butterflies and hoverflies that make do with less nectar. "People forget
that a hive is a field in the sky," she said. "Ten hives on one block can starve wild
pollinators." Her research group has counted honeybee visits to wildflowers at inner-city
parks and found more than half coming from managed hives.

The beekeeping network answered with restraint. Its regional associations declared a "no new
hives" pledge in 2019 and set up a public registry of hive locations. Signatories agree to
leave at least two seasons between placing new hives on any single block. Registry figures
show the growth of new registrations flattening out in the two years after the pledge.

The boom has also crept into classrooms. A dozen schools keep hives to teach biology, and the
first club of that kind started at a primary school in Hackney in 2016. Teachers report that
children who would not touch a science worksheet will inspect a bee hive for forty minutes.
The club's founder says the aim is not honey but attention: watching a colony work together
makes the syllabus feel closer to home.

Whether the boom lasts may depend on economics. City honey commands premium prices in local
shops, and several hotel kitchens now list its origin on their menus. As offices stand empty
and more roofs are converted to gardens, the argument over the capital's hives looks set to
continue: what one group celebrates as a golden harvest, another counts as lost flowers for
the wild things that were there first.
